anatomy.lede: A lion's mane has no brain, heart or bones: just a lobed bell of jelly, a mass of frilly arms around the mouth, and a curtain of stinging tentacles.

hotspots.label: Bell
hotspots.text: Slow pulses of the bell push the jellyfish only weakly forward, so it relies on currents to travel long distances.

hotspots.label: Bell margin
hotspots.text: In each of the eight notches between the bell's lobes sits a small balance organ that helps the jellyfish keep itself the right way up.

hotspots.label: Tentacles
hotspots.text: The tentacles hang in clusters, about 70–150 under each of the eight lobes, around 1,200 in all.

hotspots.label: Oral arms
hotspots.text: Beneath the bell, broad, frilly oral arms armed with stinging cells surround the mouth.

mind.lede: Without a brain, the lion's mane still hunts other jellies, and its prey reacts to the touch of its tentacles.

studies.title: A jellyfish that eats jellyfish
studies.text: In a Swedish fjord, lion's manes caught moon jellies, and larger lion's manes caught more of them. One moon jelly took about 38 hours to digest.

studies.title: The prey fights back
studies.text: Moon jellies that brushed a lion's mane pulled in their tentacles and pulsed 46% faster, rising away from the predator.

studies.title: Shoals
studies.text: Unusually for jellyfish, lion's manes sometimes gather in shoals up to a kilometre long.

survival.lede: A big lion's mane has little to fear, except one animal that seeks it out: the leatherback turtle.

tactics.title: A wall of stings
tactics.text: More than a thousand tentacles, each armed with stinging cells, stun prey and deter most attackers.

tactics.title: Size
tactics.text: Adults have very few natural predators because of their size, but juveniles are eaten by seabirds and larger fish such as ocean sunfish.

tactics.title: Turtle food
tactics.text: Cameras on leatherback turtles off Nova Scotia showed lion's manes made up 83–100% of their prey. Each turtle ate about 261 jellyfish a day on average.

threats.title: No major known threats
threats.text: The species is not known to face any major threats, though its population has never been assessed.

threats.title: Warming seas
threats.text: During periods of warming, some individuals may drift outside their usual range.

life.lede: The giant medusa is only one part of a life that alternates between a free-swimming bell and a tiny polyp fixed to the seabed.

stages.name: Egg and larva
stages.text: Medusae reproduce sexually. The female carries her fertilised eggs in her tentacles.

stages.name: Polyp
stages.text: The larvae settle and grow into small polyps, which multiply asexually.

stages.name: Ephyra
stages.text: Each polyp buds off a stack of tiny, immature medusae called ephyrae, which break away and swim off.

stages.name: Medusa
stages.text: The ephyrae grow into adult medusae, which are seen most often in late summer and autumn.

lifespan.value: About a year for the four stages
